beats.intro: Lesson twenty-four. [[sub]]How maturity grows, why to speed it up, and the traps that make it hard to manage this way.
beats.inside: Back to the growing child. [[same]]As the style moves from structured, to communicating, to monitoring, the amount of structure in his behaviour doesn't really change. [[teen]]A teenager knows not to ride his bike across a busy interstate. No one has to tell him any more. [[moves]]The structure has moved from being imposed from outside to being held inside.
beats.values: So teach the right way of doing things early. [[ops]]If you pass on the right operational values, your report will later decide much as you would. [[common]]Shared values, priorities and preferences, how the organization works together, are a must for the style to move along. [[confuse]]Without them, an organization gets confused and loses its sense of purpose. [[yours]]Passing them on is the supervisor's job. You are accountable for your people's output, and without shared values you cannot delegate.
beats.tuition: Grove tells of an associate who had always done outstanding work. [[hire]]He hired a junior person to take over some old tasks, and the junior did poor work. [[own]]His reaction: he has to make his own mistakes; that's how he learns. [[cust]]The trouble is, the customers pay the tuition, [[int]]whether they are inside the company or outside. [[teach]]Teaching is the supervisor's job, not a cost for customers to carry.
beats.lev: So raise your people's TRM as fast as you can. Three practical reasons. [[time]]First, the style for high TRM takes far less of your time than detailed, structured supervision. [[dele]]Second, once values are shared and TRM is high, you can delegate, and that raises your leverage. [[self]]Third, at the top, training is done and motivation comes from within: self-actualization, the strongest source of energy a manager can harness.
beats.sergeant: TRM depends on the situation, so the right style can change fast. [[camp]]Picture an army camp where nothing ever happens. The sergeant knows his soldiers well, the routines are set, and he just monitors. [[jeep]]One day a jeepload of the enemy comes over the hill, shooting. [[bark]]At once he barks orders: what to do, when, and how. [[months]]If the fighting goes on from the same place for months, it becomes routine. The group's TRM for fighting rises, [[ease]]and he gradually eases off.
beats.time: Put another way, a communicating style needs time to work. [[paper]]On paper, monitoring is a manager's most productive mode, but we have to work our way up to it. [[revert]]And when things suddenly change, we must go straight back to what, when and how. [[prej]]We feel an enlightened manager shouldn't work that way, so we take it up too late, and events overwhelm us. [[eff]]No mode is good or bad, only effective or not, for these people, in this situation. [[hour]]That is why researchers find no single best way. It changes day by day, sometimes hour by hour.
beats.q2: Quick check. Which style fits right now?
beats.extremes: Knowing all this is not enough. [[hard]]Judging someone's TRM is hard. [[pref]]And even when you know it, your own preferences tend to win. [[med]]Say a report's TRM is medium. [[ends]]In practice, the manager will likely pick structured or minimal. [[imm]]Either fully immersed in their work, making their decisions, [[alone]]or leaving them completely alone, not wanting to be bothered. [[mid]]The middle style, the one that fits, gets skipped.
beats.mirror: Another trap is how we see ourselves. [[test]]Grove asked a group of managers to rate their supervisors' style, then asked the supervisors to rate themselves. [[ninety]]Some ninety percent of the supervisors saw their style as more communicating or delegating than their subordinates did. [[why]]Partly, managers think of themselves as perfect delegators. [[sugg]]And sometimes a manager tosses out a suggestion, [[heard]]and the report hears marching orders.
beats.social: A manager once told Grove that his boss clearly had a communicating style with him, because they skied and drank together. [[wrong]]He was wrong. [[care]]A communicating style is a caring involvement in the report's work. A social relationship is something else. [[help]]A friendship off the job may help build a good relationship on the job, but don't confuse the two. [[fish]]Grove knew a boss and a report who spent a week each year fishing together in a remote place, and never talked about work. [[dist]]Their work relationship stayed distant.
beats.friends: So, should a supervisor be friends with a report? [[plus]]There are pluses: with a friend, a communicating style comes easily. [[minus]]The minus: it is harder to go back to what, when and how. Giving orders to a friend is unpleasant. [[cases]]Grove saw supervisors make a friend toe a disciplinary line. Once, the friendship was destroyed. [[ok]]Another time it worked, because the friend felt his supervisor was looking out for his career. [[test]]Grove's test: imagine giving your friend a tough performance review. If you cringe, don't make friends at work. If not, your friendships may well strengthen your work.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]As TRM grows, structure moves inside the person. [[w2]]Teach shared values yourself; don't let customers pay the tuition. [[w3]]Raise TRM fast, and go back to what, when and how when things change. [[w4]]Don't skip the middle style, and expect that you delegate less than you think. [[w5]]A friendship is not a communicating style. Try the tough-review test. Now the lesson practice.

beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of lesson twenty-four, and of Grove's chapter on task-relevant maturity.
